newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan unveils gauge for monitoring bank health.
newsitem.headline: Japan unveils gauge for monitoring bank health.

text.p: A study panel formed by Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) unveiled guidelines on Thursday for setting capital adequacy ratios that will be used to determine if a Japanese bank needs to shore up its balance sheet.

Japan's so-called prompt corrective action (PCA) system, to be introduced in April 1998, will for the first time use capital adequacy ratios as a major gauge of the soundness of financial institutions, a MOF official told reporters.
The system is designed as an early warning mechanism when a bank is facing financial troubles.
MOF was required to create the PCA system by financial laws passed this year in the wake of a series of bank collapses.

The capital adequacy ratio set under the auspices of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) will be used as a measure of the financial health of banks operating internationally, while financial institutions operating only within Japan will use a domestic standard, the official said.

The size of loan assets and uncovered potential loan losses will be assessed by the banks themselves based on guidelines to be established by auditors, and banks must set aside reserves for uncovered potential loan losses, he said.

"Because banks are strictly required to set aside loan loss provisions and write off problem loans (under the PCA system), their capital adequacy ratio might decline if their assessment of problem loans has been lax," said a member of the study group.

Under the new PCA system, the ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets in the "adequately capitalised" category will be set at four percent or more for financial institutions operating only in Japan and at eight percent or more for banks operating internationally.

If the ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets is below four percent at a bank operating only at home or below eight percent at a bank operating internationally, the institution will be required to work out a programme to boost the soundness of its operations, the MOF official said.

If the ratio is below two percent at a domestic bank or four percent at an international bank, a programme must be set up to increase capital and cut assets. Such banks would also be asked not to enter any new business activities and to restrict or halt dividend payments.

If the ratio is below zero percent, the banks will be asked to stop all or part of their business operations. This will not apply, however, to institutions if their net assets, including unrealised profits from securities holdings, exceed liabilities. Such banks would only be required to establish programmes for increasing capital and cutting assets.
